docs.title: ENUMs Reference
docs.text:
Every project-defined enum the CSharpMT4 API uses — what each one is, where it appears (a method input you pass or a reply output you read), and its values.

All enums live in the generated mt4_term_api namespace. Reference a member as mt4_term_api.EnumName.Member:

using mt4_term_api;

var req = new OrderSendRequest { Symbol = "EURUSD", OperationType = OrderSendOperationType.OcOpBuy };
var bars = await service.BarsAsync("EURUSD", QUOTE_HISTORY_TIMEFRAME.QhbPeriodH1, from, to);

Enums print with their C# member name via ToString(); the numeric value is the proto wire value.

docs.title: 🔎 Quick lookup — which methods touch enums
docs.text: Method Input enum Output enum AccountSummaryAsync — EnumAccountTradeMode, EnumAccountMarginMode QuoteHistoryAsync ENUM_QUOTE_HISTORY_TIMEFRAME — BarsAsync QUOTE_HISTORY_TIMEFRAME — SymbolParamsManyAsync — SP_ENUM_SYMBOL_TRADE_MODE, SP_ENUM_SYMBOL_TRADE_EXECUTION, SP_ENUM_TRADE_CALC_MODE ServerTimezoneAsync — SERVER_TIMEZONE_SOURCE OpenedOrdersAsync EnumOpenedOrderSortType OpenedOrderType (per order) OrdersHistoryAsync EnumOrderHistorySortType OpenedOrderType (per order) OrderSendAsync OrderSendOperationType — OrderCloseDeleteAsync — OrderCloseDeleteMode OnTradeAsync / OnOpenedOrdersProfitAsync — MT4_SUB_ENUM_EVENT_GROUP_TYPE (+ SUB_ORDER_OPERATION_TYPE per order)

docs.title: EnumAccountMarginMode — AccountSummaryData.AccountMarginMode (out)
docs.text:
• AccountMarginModeRetailNetting = 0 — one net position per symbol
  • AccountMarginModeExchange = 1 — exchange model
  • AccountMarginModeRetailHedging = 2 — hedging (the usual MT4 model)

docs.title: QUOTE_HISTORY_TIMEFRAME — BarsAsync(timeframe) (in)
docs.text: Members are the period in minutes (different enum from the one above — don't mix): * QhbPeriodM1 = 1 · QhbPeriodM5 = 5 · QhbPeriodM15 = 15 · QhbPeriodM30 = 30 * QhbPeriodH1 = 60 · QhbPeriodH4 = 240 · QhbPeriodD1 = 1440 · QhbPeriodW1 = 10080 · QhbPeriodMn1 = 43200 * QhbPeriodUnspecified = 0 (do not use)

docs.title: OrderSendOperationType — OrderSendRequest.OperationType (in)
docs.text:
• OcOpBuy = 0 · OcOpSell = 1 — market
  • OcOpBuylimit = 2 · OcOpSelllimit = 3 — pending limit
  • OcOpBuystop = 4 · OcOpSellstop = 5 — pending stop

Casing: pending members are OcOpBuylimit / OcOpSelllimit / OcOpBuystop / OcOpSellstop (lowercase after Op).

docs.title: OpenedOrderType — OpenedOrderInfo.OrderType / HistoryOrderInfo.OrderType (out)
docs.text:
• OoOpBuy = 0 · OoOpSell = 1 — market
  • OoOpBuylimit = 2 · OoOpSelllimit = 3 — pending limit
  • OoOpBuystop = 4 · OoOpSellstop = 5 — pending stop
  • OoOpBalance = 6 · OoOpCredit = 7 — ledger entries (deposit/withdrawal, credit)

docs.title: OrderCloseDeleteMode — OrderCloseDeleteData.Mode (out)
docs.text:
• OcdMarketOrder = 0 — a market order was closed
  • OcdPendingOrder = 1 — a pending order was deleted

docs.title: MT4_SUB_ENUM_EVENT_GROUP_TYPE — OnTradeData.Type / OnOpenedOrdersProfitData.Type (out)
docs.text:
• OrderProfit = 0 — periodic profit/price update for open orders
  • OrderUpdate = 1 — an order was created / modified / closed

docs.title: ⚠️ Errors
docs.text: Errors are surfaced as ApiExceptionMT4 (its Error carries the detail); they are not numeric return codes.

docs.title: ErrorType — Error.ErrorType
docs.text: Classifies where an error came from, e.g.: * Undefined = 0 · Mrpc = 1 · MrpcValidation = 2 · MrpcTimeout = 3 * TerminalApiTimeout = 4 · TerminalApiGetParams = 5 · TerminalApiSetResult = 6 · TerminalApiUnexpected = 7 * MqlExecution = 8 · MqlCustomExecution = 9

docs.title: MqlErrorCode
docs.text:
The MT4/MQL trade error code set (many values) carried on execution errors — inspect ApiExceptionMT4 fields (MqlErrorCode / MqlErrorDescription) when a trade is rejected. See Return Codes.

Not listed here are terminal-management enums (ChartTemplateMode, EA_PARAM_TYPE, TerminalType, GUI/proxy enums, …) — they belong to terminal-control features outside the core trading/data API documented in these guides.

docs.title: Getting Started with CSharpMT4
docs.text: Quick Setup & Overview - Start automating your trading with CSharpMT4 (C# for MetaTrader 4) in minutes.

docs.title: 🎯 What is CSharpMT4?
docs.text: CSharpMT4 is an industrial-grade, type-safe C# client library for interacting with MetaTrader 4 terminals via high-performance gRPC. It eliminates complex C++ DLL wrappers and provides direct, reliable programmatic trading.

docs.title: 🌟 Key Advantages
docs.text:
• High Throughput: Native gRPC streaming for sub-millisecond price ticks and trade execution.
  • Three-Layer Architecture: Low-level gRPC (MT4Account), typed wrapper methods (MT4Service), and high-level convenience (MT4Sugar).
  • Resilient Connection: Auto-reconnect, exponential backoff, and transparent channel healing.
  • Production Ready: Fully verified across institutional accounts, hedge fund systems, and automated retail bots.

docs.title: 📦 Installation
docs.text:
Install CSharpMT4 via your standard C# package manager:

dotnet add package MetaRPC.MT4

This pulls the published NuGet package MetaRPC.MT4 from nuget.org — the generated gRPC clients plus the MT4Account low-level wrapper. That is all your own app needs.

ℹ️ This repository is the examples/demo project, not the package itself. It references the SDK from the local package/ folder (<ProjectReference ... package\MetaRPC.MT4.csproj />), so it compiles against that source. Any local edit here lives in this repo only — it is not in what dotnet add package downloads unless it is published as a new NuGet version. Your own project should just dotnet add package MetaRPC.MT4.

docs.title: 🔑 API Key & Authentication
docs.text:
Connecting to MetaRPC production endpoints (mt4.mrpc.pro:443) requires an API key:

  1. Sign Up: Create an account for free at https://mrpc.pro/signup.
  2. Generate API Key: In your MetaRPC Portal dashboard at https://mrpc.pro/my, go to API Keys to generate and copy your personal API token.
  3. Configure Connection: Pass your API key / token along with the server address (mt4.mrpc.pro:443) in your connection settings.

docs.title: ⚙️ Configuration — provide your connection data
docs.text:
The SDK requires your connection settings. It reads them in this order and falls back to the built-in defaults only if none are set:

1) Command line / environment variables (highest priority)

  • --api-key <key> (or the first positional argument) → API key.
  • MRPC_API_KEY → API key.
  • MT4Options__User, MT4Options__Password, MT4Options__ServerName, MT4Options__Grpc, MT4Options__Symbol, MT4Options__ApiKey → any setting (the double underscore is the nested-key separator).

2) appsettings.json → section MT4Options

{
  "MT4Options": {
    "User": 0,
    "Password": "<your password>",
    "ServerName": "<broker server, e.g. MetaQuotes-Demo>",
    "Grpc": "https://mt4.mrpc.pro:443",
    "ApiKey": "<your API key>",
    "Symbol": "EURUSD"
  }
}

3) Built-in defaults (last resort) — Grpc → production https://mt4.mrpc.pro:443, ApiKey → TRIAL.

⚠️ Set Grpc explicitly for any non-production environment. If you test against a different MetaRPC endpoint (for example staging https://mt4-stg.mrpc.pro:443) and do not set Grpc, the SDK silently falls back to production and the terminal won't connect where you expect. Always provide User, Password, ServerName, Grpc and ApiKey — via environment or appsettings.json — before connecting.

If User is 0 or the password is blank, the SDK tries to auto-provision a demo on the configured endpoint; that requires a non-TRIAL API key.

docs.title: ▶️ How to Run
docs.text:
There are two different scenarios, and it matters which one you're in:

A. Run this repository B. Use the SDK in your own project Goal Explore the SDK — see every call run, try the strategies Build your own bot You get it by git clone this repo dotnet add package MetaRPC.MT4 Entry point the example menu (12 ready-made demos) your own Program.cs Config appsettings.json / env (see above) however you like — constructor args, env, your own config The --example / menu flags ✅ live here ❌ not part of the package

docs.title: A. Run this repository (the examples / demo project)
docs.text:
Clone, then run. On start it loads your configuration, connects, and shows a menu of 12 demos (the three API tiers, the orchestrators, the preset, the sandbox, and the protobuf inspector).

git clone https://github.com/MetaRPC/CSharpMT4.git
cd CSharpMT4
dotnet run                      # interactive menu (pick 1–12, a = all, q = quit)

The menu that appears:

# Entry What it runs 1 LOW-LEVEL: info MT4Account read calls — account, symbols, orders 2 LOW-LEVEL: trading MT4Account send/modify/close flow (guarded — described unless enabled) 3 LOW-LEVEL: streaming All five MT4Account streams, sampled a few seconds each 4 SERVICE suite (all) Every MT4Service group, read-only 5 SUGAR scenario MT4Sugar assess → plan → execute lifecycle (guarded) 6 ORCHESTRATOR: scalp Risk-sized entry + TP + timed exit (described) 7 ORCHESTRATOR: trailing stop Entry protected by a trailing stop (described) 8 ORCHESTRATOR: grid Symmetric pending-order grid (described) 9 ORCHESTRATOR: breakout Buy/sell-stop straddle (described) 10 PRESET: adaptive mode Picks scalp or trailing from live conditions (described) 11 USER CODE sandbox Your own scratch example, pre-connected 12 PROTOBUF inspector Explore the generated proto types (no connection needed) a Run ALL Run every entry in order q Quit Exit

The orchestrators, preset and sugar/trading demos are described (dry-run) by default — they print their plan and send nothing until you turn trading on. See Strategies.

Pick demos non-interactively instead of using the menu — everything after -- is passed to the program, not to dotnet run:

dotnet run -- --example=1       # one demo by number (1–12)
dotnet run -- --example=sugar   # ...or by a substring of its name
dotnet run -- --all             # run the whole suite in order
dotnet run -- --inspect         # protobuf inspector only — no connection needed
dotnet run -- --api-key <KEY>   # supply the API key on the command line

ℹ️ Piped / redirected stdin (CI) runs the whole suite automatically, so nothing hangs waiting for menu input.

docs.title: B. Use the SDK in your own project
docs.text:
You do not clone this repo. Add the package, write your own entry point (the Minimal Connection Example below), and run it:

dotnet add package MetaRPC.MT4
dotnet run

There is no menu and appsettings.json is not required — you pass user, password, serverName, grpcServer and apiKey into new MT4Account(...) however your app prefers. The example menu and the --example flags belong to this repository only.

docs.title: What the package actually gives you
docs.text:
dotnet add package MetaRPC.MT4 pulls three layers stacked on the raw protocol:

MT4Sugar    ← high-level convenience (risk sizing, normalization, one-liners)
MT4Service  ← typed, data-returning wrappers
MT4Account  ← low-level gRPC calls (connect, session id, retries, streams)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
generated gRPC / protobuf stubs   ← the raw proto contract

You normally call MT4Account / MT4Service / MT4Sugar. You can drop down to the generated protobuf clients directly, but the wrappers exist precisely so you don't have to hand-build requests, attach the APIKey/session-id headers, or write reconnect logic yourself. Cloning this repo gives you those layers plus the runnable examples; adding the package gives you the layers only.

docs.title: 🆔 Automatic Account ID & Authentication
docs.text:
MetaRPC endpoints require authentication and session management:

  1. APIKey: Your personal authentication token from https://mrpc.pro/my (obtained by registering at https://mrpc.pro/signup). Sent in the APIKey header.

  2. id: A terminal session GUID returned by Connect / ConnectEx (terminalInstanceGuid).

💡 Seamless Automation: You do not need to call GetId or provide an id header when connecting. The server automatically generates a session GUID upon connection and returns it to the caller. The SDK automatically captures this session ID and attaches it alongside your APIKey to all subsequent requests and streaming subscriptions.

docs.title: 🔌 Minimal Connection Example
docs.text:
Here is how easy it is to initialize MT4Account, connect to your MetaTrader terminal, and retrieve your account balance:

var account = new MT4Account(user, password, grpcServer, apiKey);
// defaults: waitForTerminalIsAlive = true, timeoutSeconds = 30
await account.ConnectByServerNameAsync(serverName, "EURUSD");
var summary = await account.AccountSummaryAsync();
Console.WriteLine($"Balance: {summary.AccountBalance}, Equity: {summary.AccountEquity}");

docs.title: 🗺️ Documentation Road Map
docs.text:
To get the most out of CSharpMT4, follow this suggested reading order:

  1. Your First Project - Build and run a working project in 10 minutes.
  2. Project Map - Understand the 3 architectural layers and interaction flow.
  3. Glossary - Essential MetaTrader 4 and algorithmic trading terminology.
  4. MT4 for Beginners - Step-by-step terminal setup and demo account guide.
  5. gRPC Streaming - Subscribe to ticks, trades, DOM, and position updates.
  6. Return Codes - Complete reference of broker and gateway return codes.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Terms and concepts used across the CSharpMT4 SDK and these docs. Short, practical definitions — follow the links for detail.

docs.title: 🏛️ Architecture
docs.text:
MT4Account — the low-level layer. Direct gRPC/protobuf calls: you build a Request and read a Reply.Data. Full control, most verbose. Source: package/Helpers/MT4Account.cs. Docs: MT4Account.

MT4Service — the mid-level layer. A typed facade over MT4Account that forwards the data methods 1:1 and adds convenience getters. Docs: MT4Service.

MT4Sugar — the high-level layer. Extension methods on MT4Service: snapshots, normalization, risk sizing, one-line market orders, bulk close. Docs: MT4Sugar.

Layer rule of thumb — Sugar for one-liners → Service for typed data → Account for raw request/reply.

docs.title: 🔌 gRPC & protobuf
docs.text:
gRPC — the RPC protocol the SDK speaks to the MetaRPC gateway over HTTP/2 + TLS.

Protobuf — the message format. Every call has a generated XxxRequest and XxxReply; the payload lives in Reply.Data (an XxxData object).

Service / Method — the gRPC service (e.g. mt4_term_api.AccountHelper) and its method (e.g. AccountSummary(AccountSummaryRequest) → AccountSummaryReply).

Unary vs streaming — most calls are unary (one request → one reply). Subscriptions are server-streaming: the SDK exposes them as IAsyncEnumerable<T> consumed with await foreach.

Timestamp — google.protobuf.Timestamp. All times are UTC; prefer the *Utc fields where a reply exposes both.

docs.title: 🔑 Connection & auth
docs.text:
gRPC endpoint (Grpc) — the gateway URL, e.g. production https://mt4.mrpc.pro:443 or staging https://mt4-stg.mrpc.pro:443. Set it explicitly per environment — see Configuration.

ServerName — the broker server to attach to (e.g. MetaQuotes-Demo, EGlobal-Demo). Used by ConnectByServerNameAsync.

Host / Port — an optional direct connection path (ConnectByHostPortAsync) instead of a server name.

ApiKey — your MetaRPC token, sent in the APIKey header. TRIAL is the limited default (cannot open demo accounts).

terminalInstanceGuid / session id — a session GUID the gateway generates on connect and returns; the SDK attaches it to later calls automatically. You do not call GetId before connecting.

Terminal "alive" / readiness — after connecting, the terminal instance must be alive before it serves data. The connect helpers do a KICK (spin up) → WAIT (require alive) sequence with retries.

Auto-provision (demo) — if User is 0 or the password is blank, the SDK tries to open a demo account on the configured endpoint (needs a non-TRIAL key).

docs.title: 💰 Account
docs.text:
Balance — funds excluding floating P/L. Equity — balance + floating P/L of open orders.

Margin / Free margin — margin currently used / available for new orders. Margin level — (Equity / Margin) × 100 percent.

Leverage — e.g. 100 for 1:100. Currency — the deposit currency (money fields are denominated in it). Credit — credit amount.

Trade mode — EnumAccountTradeMode: demo / contest / real. Margin mode — EnumAccountMarginMode: netting / exchange / hedging (the usual MT4 model).

docs.title: 📈 Symbols & prices
docs.text:
Symbol — an instrument name (e.g. EURUSD). Brokers may add suffixes (EURUSD.r) — use the exact name from SymbolsAsync().

Bid / Ask — best sell / buy price. Spread — Ask − Bid; the SDK's GetSpreadAsync returns it in points (computed from a quote).

Digits — decimal places in the price. Point — the smallest price step, 10^-digits (e.g. 0.00001 for a 5-digit symbol).

Point vs pip — on 3/5-digit symbols 1 pip = 10 points. PointsToPipsAsync converts.

Volume (lots) — order size. VolumeMin / VolumeMax / VolumeStep — broker limits; snap your size to them (NormalizeVolumeAsync).

Tick value / tick size / contract size — money per tick, minimal price increment, units per lot — inputs for P/L and risk sizing (TickValueWithSizeAsync).

Timeframe — bar period. QuoteHistoryAsync uses ENUM_QUOTE_HISTORY_TIMEFRAME (Qh*); BarsAsync uses QUOTE_HISTORY_TIMEFRAME (Qhb*) — don't mix the two.

docs.title: 📦 Orders & trading
docs.text:
Order — MT4 works with orders (not netted positions). Each has a ticket (unique int id).

Market order — fills now at Bid/Ask. Pending order — waits at a target price: buy/sell limit or stop.

Order type (open) — OpenedOrderType: OoOpBuy, OoOpSell, OoOpBuylimit, OoOpSelllimit, OoOpBuystop, OoOpSellstop (+ OoOpBalance/OoOpCredit ledger entries).

Operation type (send) — OrderSendOperationType: OcOpBuy/OcOpSell (market) or OcOpBuylimit/OcOpBuystop/OcOpSelllimit/OcOpSellstop (pending).

SL / TP — stop-loss / take-profit, as absolute prices (points-based helpers exist in Sugar).

Slippage — max allowed price deviation on a market order, in points.

Magic number — an int tag to identify an order's strategy/EA.

Close vs delete — closing a market order vs deleting a pending one. OrderCloseDeleteData.Mode (OrderCloseDeleteMode) says which happened. Close-by — close one order with an opposite one (hedged accounts).

docs.title: 📡 Streaming
docs.text:
Subscription — a server stream of events, returned as IAsyncEnumerable<T>. Always pass a CancellationToken; cancelling completes it gracefully (a Cancelled status is normal).

Event group — MT4_SUB_ENUM_EVENT_GROUP_TYPE (OrderProfit periodic update / OrderUpdate create-modify-close) on trade/profit streams.

Snapshot semantics — profit/ticket streams emit the current set each interval; compute add/remove diffs on the client.

Guide: gRPC Streaming.

docs.title: ⚠️ Errors & resilience
docs.text:
ApiExceptionMT4 — thrown when the gateway returns an error (carries the broker/terminal detail). Not a numeric return code.

Reconnection — unary calls retry on transient gRPC statuses (Unavailable, DeadlineExceeded, Internal) and reconnectable terminal errors, with exponential backoff; streams restart with backoff.

Deadline — an absolute per-call UTC cut-off (deadline) that converts to a timeout. CancellationToken — cooperative cancel for a call or a stream.

docs.title: 📝 Conventions in these docs
docs.text: *Data — a protobuf reply payload (e.g. AccountSummaryData). *Async — the async method; most have a synchronous twin without the suffix. Getter (GetBalanceAsync, …) — a MT4Service shortcut returning a single value.

docs.title: 📡 gRPC Streaming & Subscription Management
docs.text:
Complete guide to real-time subscriptions in the C# MT4 SDK — how to open a stream, how to stop it cleanly, and how the built-in reconnect loop keeps it alive.

This document covers:

  • ✅ How to subscribe to real-time market/account data
  • ✅ How to stop a stream without leaking connections
  • ✅ Patterns from a 10-second sample to a long-running background service
  • ✅ Architecture — the reconnect loop and its safety guarantees
  • ✅ Troubleshooting and best practices

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. Quick Start
  2. Available Streaming Methods
  3. How Stopping Works in C#
  4. Patterns (simple → advanced)
  5. Common Mistakes
  6. Streaming with Enums
  7. Architecture & Safety
  8. Troubleshooting

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Every streaming method returns an IAsyncEnumerable<T>. You consume it with await foreach, and you stop it with a CancellationToken. That is the whole model.

using System;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

// acc is a connected MT4Account (see Getting Started for how to connect).
// Stream EURUSD ticks for 10 seconds, then stop automatically.
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10));

try
{
    await foreach (var data in acc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }, cts.Token))
    {
        var t = data.SymbolTick;
        Console.WriteLine($"{t.Symbol}  Bid={t.Bid}  Ask={t.Ask}  @ {t.Time}");
    }
}
catch (OperationCanceledException)
{
    // Expected when the token fires — the stream was asked to stop.
}

Console.WriteLine("Stream finished.");

What happens here

  • CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan) cancels itself after 10 s (same as calling CancelAfter).
  • When the token fires, the stream ends and await foreach throws OperationCanceledException, which we swallow.
  • using disposes the CancellationTokenSource; leaving the foreach disposes the underlying gRPC call. No channel to close per stream — the connection belongs to the account.

🟢 When to use: quick tests, short monitoring windows, examples.

docs.title: Available Streaming Methods
docs.text: All of these return IAsyncEnumerable<T> and are driven by a CancellationToken.

docs.title: On MT4Account (low-level)
docs.text: Method Yields What it pushes OnSymbolTickAsync(IEnumerable<string> symbols, ct) OnSymbolTickData A message on every tick of the subscribed symbol(s) — .SymbolTick has Symbol, Bid, Ask, Time. OnTradeAsync(ct) OnTradeData Order create / modify / close events on the account. OnOpenedOrdersProfitAsync(int intervalMs, ct) OnOpenedOrdersProfitData Live P/L snapshot every intervalMs — .OpenedOrdersWithProfitUpdated, .AccountInfo?.Equity. OnOpenedOrdersTicketsAsync(int intervalMs, ct) OnOpenedOrdersTicketsData The set of open tickets every intervalMs — .PositionTickets (lighter than the profit stream). OnConnectStateAsync(ct) ConnectStateData Terminal link state — fires when the connection drops or returns.

docs.title: On MT4Service (typed facade)
docs.text:
MT4Service re-exposes the same five methods with the same signatures (intervalMs defaults to 1000), so you can stream straight from the service you already use for everything else.

It also adds two sugar readers for the two most common streams:

Method Yields Notes ReadTicks(string symbol, ct) OnSymbolTickData Single-symbol tick reader — thin wrapper over OnSymbolTickAsync. ReadTrades(ct) OnTradeData Trade-event reader — thin wrapper over OnTradeAsync.

Live examples in the repo:

  • examples/LowLevel/3_Streaming.cs — all five low-level streams, each sampled ~3 s.
  • examples/Services/4_ServiceExamples.cs — the Subscriptions section streams the same five from MT4Service.
  • examples/Sugar/5_SugarScenario.cs — ReadTicks / ReadTrades inside the ASSESS step.

docs.title: How Stopping Works in C
docs.text: There are two ways a stream ends, and they are not the same:

docs.title: 1. break out of the await foreach — clean, but only between items
docs.text:
When you break (or return, or throw) out of an await foreach, the compiler disposes the async enumerator. That runs the stream's internal finally, which disposes the gRPC call — so there is no orphaned background loop (unlike some other runtimes, C# iterators stop when iteration stops).

int n = 0;
await foreach (var data in acc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }, ct))
{
    if (++n >= 10) break;   // clean: the enumerator is disposed, the call is released
    Console.WriteLine(data.SymbolTick.Bid);
}

⚠️ The catch: break can only run after an item is delivered. If the market goes quiet, the loop is parked inside MoveNext waiting for the next message and your break never gets a turn. For a stream that may idle, use a token.

docs.title: 2. Cancel the CancellationToken — prompt, works even when idle
docs.text:
Cancelling the token unblocks the pending MoveNext immediately, so the stream stops now, whether or not another message ever arrives. This is why every example drives streams with a token.

using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
cts.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));   // or cts.Cancel() from elsewhere

try
{
    await foreach (var data in acc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }, cts.Token))
        Console.WriteLine(data.SymbolTick.Bid);
}
catch (OperationCanceledException) { /* expected on cancel */ }

🔑 Rule of thumb: use a token to bound when a stream stops; use break to stop on a data condition. They compose — see the patterns below.

docs.title: The reusable sampling helper
docs.text:
The examples factor this into one small helper you can copy. It opens a stream, prints up to maxItems, and auto-stops after seconds — using a linked token so an outer cancellation still propagates:

static async Task Sample<T>(
    Func<CancellationToken, IAsyncEnumerable<T>> make,
    CancellationToken outer,
    Action<int, T> print,
    int seconds = 3,
    int maxItems = 3)
{
    using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(outer);
    cts.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(seconds));

    int n = 0;
    try
    {
        await foreach (var x in make(cts.Token))
        {
            print(++n, x);
            if (n >= maxItems) break;
        }
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) { }   // timeout/cancel is expected
    Console.WriteLine($"  ({n} event(s))");
}

// Usage:
await Sample(c => acc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }, c), ct,
             (i, d) => Console.WriteLine($"tick #{i}: {d.SymbolTick.Bid}"));

docs.title: Pattern 1 — Timeout window
docs.text:
Stop after a fixed time. Simplest possible bound.

using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10));
try
{
    await foreach (var d in svc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }, cts.Token))
        Console.WriteLine(d.SymbolTick.Bid);
}
catch (OperationCanceledException) { }

docs.title: Pattern 2 — Event-limited
docs.text:
Stop after N messages (token still there as a safety net in case the market is quiet).

using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(60));
int count = 0;
try
{
    await foreach (var d in svc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }, cts.Token))
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{++count}] {d.SymbolTick.Symbol} {d.SymbolTick.Bid}");
        if (count >= 100) break;
    }
}
catch (OperationCanceledException) { }

docs.title: Pattern 3 — Condition-based stop
docs.text:
Stop when the data meets a condition.

using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
try
{
    await foreach (var d in svc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }, cts.Token))
    {
        var bid = d.SymbolTick.Bid;
        Console.WriteLine($"Price: {bid}");
        if (bid > 1.10000) { Console.WriteLine("Target reached!"); break; }
    }
}
catch (OperationCanceledException) { }

docs.title: Pattern 4 — Background service with manual control
docs.text:
Run a stream on its own Task and stop it on demand from elsewhere. The CancellationTokenSource is the off-switch.

public sealed class PriceMonitor
{
    private readonly MT4Service _svc;
    private readonly CancellationTokenSource _cts = new();
    private Task? _task;

    public PriceMonitor(MT4Service svc) => _svc = svc;

    public void Start(string[] symbols) => _task = Task.Run(() => LoopAsync(symbols));

    private async Task LoopAsync(string[] symbols)
    {
        try
        {
            await foreach (var d in _svc.OnSymbolTickAsync(symbols, _cts.Token))
                Console.WriteLine($"{d.SymbolTick.Symbol}: {d.SymbolTick.Bid} / {d.SymbolTick.Ask}");
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException) { }   // normal shutdown
    }

    public async Task StopAsync()
    {
        _cts.Cancel();                 // signal the stream to stop
        if (_task != null) await _task; // wait for the loop to unwind
        _cts.Dispose();
    }
}

// Usage:
var monitor = new PriceMonitor(svc);
monitor.Start(new[] { "EURUSD", "GBPUSD" });
await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
await monitor.StopAsync();

docs.title: Pattern 5 — Multiple concurrent streams
docs.text:
Run several streams at once and stop all of them with a single token. Give each its own try/catch so one failing stream doesn't tear down the others, and await them together.

using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)); // stops all after 30 s

async Task Ticks()
{
    try { await foreach (var d in svc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }, cts.Token))
              Console.WriteLine($"[TICK] {d.SymbolTick.Bid}"); }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) { }
}

async Task Trades()
{
    try { await foreach (var d in svc.OnTradeAsync(cts.Token))
              Console.WriteLine($"[TRADE] {d}"); }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) { }
}

async Task Profits()
{
    try { await foreach (var d in svc.OnOpenedOrdersProfitAsync(2000, cts.Token))
              Console.WriteLine($"[PROFIT] {d.OpenedOrdersWithProfitUpdated.Count} order(s), equity={d.AccountInfo?.Equity}"); }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) { }
}

await Task.WhenAll(Ticks(), Trades(), Profits());
Console.WriteLine("All streams stopped.");

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 1 — Streaming without a token
docs.text:
// If the market goes quiet, there is no way to stop this loop promptly.
await foreach (var d in acc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }))
{
    if (count >= 10) break;   // only runs when the NEXT tick arrives
}

✅ Fix: pass a token so you can stop even when no item is pending.

using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
await foreach (var d in acc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }, cts.Token)) { /* ... */ }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 2 — Letting OperationCanceledException escape
docs.text:
Cancelling a stream throws OperationCanceledException (or TaskCanceledException). That is normal; don't let it crash your app.

try { await foreach (var d in svc.OnTradeAsync(cts.Token)) { /* ... */ } }
catch (OperationCanceledException) { /* expected on stop */ }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 3 — One CancellationTokenSource reused after cancel
docs.text:
A CancellationTokenSource is single-use: once cancelled, every token from it is already cancelled. To start a new stream, create a new source.

// ❌ cts was cancelled earlier → this stream ends immediately
await foreach (var d in svc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }, cts.Token)) { }

// ✅ fresh source per run
using var cts2 = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
await foreach (var d in svc.OnSymbolTickAsync(new[] { "EURUSD" }, cts2.Token)) { }

docs.title: ❌ Mistake 4 — Heavy work inside the loop body
docs.text: The loop body runs on the consuming task; slow work there backs up the stream. Hand off heavy processing (queue it, or Task.Run the CPU-bound part) and keep the loop tight.

docs.title: Streaming with Enums
docs.text:
Some stream payloads carry MT4 enum fields you can filter on. The two that matter for subscriptions:

Enum Where it appears MT4_SUB_ENUM_EVENT_GROUP_TYPE OnTradeData.Type / OnOpenedOrdersProfitData.Type — which kind of event this message represents. SUB_ORDER_OPERATION_TYPE OnOpenedOrdersProfitOrderInfo.Type — the operation type of each order in a profit snapshot.

Example — react only to a specific trade-event group:

using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));
try
{
    await foreach (var ev in svc.OnTradeAsync(cts.Token))
    {
        // ev.Type is an MT4_SUB_ENUM_EVENT_GROUP_TYPE value — switch on it to route events.
        Console.WriteLine($"event group: {ev.Type}");
    }
}
catch (OperationCanceledException) { }

See ENUMs Reference → Streaming for the full list of streaming enums and their members.

docs.title: One mechanism behind every stream
docs.text:
All five low-level streams funnel through a single private helper on MT4Account:

OnSymbolTickAsync / OnTradeAsync / OnOpenedOrdersProfitAsync / ...
        │
        ▼
ExecuteStreamWithReconnect<TRequest, TReply, TData>   (the reconnect loop)
        │
        ▼
gRPC server-streaming call  ──►  Network  ──►  MT4 terminal

Because every stream shares this helper, the lifecycle rules are identical for all of them: the same cancellation behavior, the same reconnect behavior, the same cleanup.

docs.title: What the reconnect loop guarantees
docs.text:
ExecuteStreamWithReconnect runs roughly:

while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)          // token is the only way out
{
    AsyncServerStreamingCall<TReply>? call = null;
    try
    {
        call = streamInvoker(request, headers, ct);
        while (await call.ResponseStream.MoveNext(ct))
            yield return data;               // hand each message to your foreach
    }
    catch (RpcException ex) when (transient)  // Unavailable / DeadlineExceeded / Internal
    {
        needReconnect = true;                 // drop out, reconnect, open a NEW stream
    }
    finally
    {
        call?.Dispose();                      // ✅ the current call is ALWAYS released
    }

    if (needReconnect) { await Reconnect(); } // transparent to your loop
    else break;
}

✅ What it does for you

  • Auto-reconnect on transient transport errors (Unavailable, DeadlineExceeded, Internal) and on reconnectable API errors — your await foreach keeps delivering across a blip, up to a restart cap.
  • Always disposes the current gRPC call in finally, so a dropped or finished stream never leaks.
  • Clean completion — cancellation-by-token, server-sent Cancelled, and end-of-stream (EOF) all end the enumeration gracefully (yield break).

⚠️ What you must do

  • Provide and control a CancellationToken. The loop exits only when the token is cancelled (or the server finalizes the stream). Without cancellation a healthy stream runs indefinitely — which is correct for a long-running service, but means you own the off-switch.
  • Expect OperationCanceledException when you cancel, and catch it.
  • A non-transient API error surfaces as ApiExceptionMT4 out of the await foreach — handle it like any other call's error (see Return Codes).

docs.title: Connection vs. stream
docs.text: A stream does not own the connection. You connect once (e.g. via ConnectionHelper/MT4Account), open and close as many streams as you like over that connection, and disconnect once at the end. There is no per-stream channel.close().

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix Stream never stops on break Market is quiet; loop is parked in MoveNext Drive it with a CancellationToken (CancelAfter / Cancel). OperationCanceledException crashes the app Not caught around the await foreach Wrap the loop in try { } catch (OperationCanceledException) { }. New stream ends immediately Reusing an already-cancelled CancellationTokenSource Create a new CancellationTokenSource per run. Stream keeps dropping and reopening Transient transport errors being auto-retried Usually fine (that's the reconnect loop). If persistent, check network / server endpoint in config. ApiExceptionMT4 out of the loop Server sent a non-transient, non-final error Inspect the error code; see Return Codes. Lagging / backed-up stream Heavy work in the loop body Keep the body tight; offload processing.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• MT4Account — API Reference — low-level streaming methods.
  • MT4Service — API Reference — the typed streaming facade.
  • MT4Sugar — API Reference — ReadTicks / ReadTrades.
  • ENUMs Reference — streaming enums.
  • Return Codes — handling ApiExceptionMT4 from a stream.

Remember: streams are IAsyncEnumerable<T> you read with await foreach; a CancellationToken is your off-switch; the SDK reconnects and disposes for you. Own the token, catch the cancel, and your streaming code stays leak-free. 🚀

docs.title: 🧭 MT4 for Beginners: Your First Steps
docs.text: Welcome! This guide is for complete beginners — never touched MetaTrader 4 or trading before. It explains what MT4 is, how to create a free demo account in the terminal, and where to go next to drive it from C# with CSharpMT4.

docs.title: 🖥️ What is MetaTrader 4 (MT4)?
docs.text:
MetaTrader 4 is a trading platform used by millions of traders worldwide. With it you can:

  • Trade forex, metals, commodities and more
  • Analyze markets with charts and indicators
  • Run automated trading strategies
  • Monitor your positions in real time

Think of MT4 as the cockpit for the markets. CSharpMT4 lets you drive that cockpit programmatically from C# over gRPC — reading prices, placing orders, streaming ticks — without clicking around the terminal by hand.

docs.title: Why start with a demo account?
docs.text:
A demo account is a risk-free practice account funded with virtual money. Start here — always:

  • ✅ Zero risk — virtual funds (typically $10,000–$100,000)
  • ✅ Real market conditions — live prices and behavior
  • ✅ Learn the platform — before any real money is involved
  • ✅ Perfect for testing — develop and run your CSharpMT4 code against it

docs.title: Live account
docs.text: A live account uses real money. Only move to live once you understand MT4, have tested your strategy thoroughly on demo, and accept the risks.

docs.title: 🚀 Creating a demo account in MT4
docs.text: You need an account (login, password, server) for the SDK to connect to. Here's the full walk-through in the terminal.

docs.title: Step 1️⃣ — Download & install MT4
docs.text: Get the terminal from your broker, or the MetaTrader site: https://www.metatrader4.com/en/download. Install it for your OS.

docs.title: Step 2️⃣ — Find the Navigator panel
docs.text:
On launch, MT4 often shows an "open an account" popup. If not, find the Navigator panel (left side, below Market Watch).

Inside Navigator you'll see Accounts, Indicators, Expert Advisors, and more.

docs.title: Step 3️⃣ — Open a new demo account
docs.text: In Navigator, right-click on Accounts → "Open an account". This opens the broker-server search.

docs.title: Step 4️⃣ — Select the demo server
docs.text: Find "MetaQuotes-Demo" (the standard demo server) in the list — use the search box if needed — select it and click Next.

docs.title: Step 5️⃣ — Choose "Open a new demo account"
Step 6️⃣ — Fill in your details
docs.text: Name, email, account type, deposit (e.g. $10,000), leverage (1:100 is fine), currency. Accept the terms and click Next.

docs.title: Step 7️⃣ — Save your credentials
docs.text:
MT4 shows your Login, Password, Investor Password and Server (e.g. MetaQuotes-Demo).

⚠️ Save these immediately — you'll need the login, password and server name for the config below.

docs.title: ⚙️ Connect CSharpMT4 to your demo account
docs.text:
Put the credentials MT4 gave you into the MT4Options section of appsettings.json:

{
  "MT4Options": {
    "User": 591129415,
    "Password": "YourPasswordHere",
    "ServerName": "MetaQuotes-Demo",
    "Grpc": "https://mt4.mrpc.pro:443",
    "ApiKey": "<your API key>",
    "Symbol": "EURUSD"
  }
}
  • User — your login number.
  • Password — your master password.
  • ServerName — the exact server name from MT4 (e.g. MetaQuotes-Demo).
  • Grpc — the MetaRPC endpoint (leave as is for production).
  • ApiKey — your key from https://mrpc.pro/my.

Full precedence rules (env → appsettings → defaults) and API-key details are in Getting Started → Configuration.

Then run dotnet run — the console prints the resolved config and a CONNECT box. A successful connect means you're ready to go.

docs.title: Master password
docs.text:
• Full access — open/close trades, change settings.
  • The one you created during registration.
  • This is the password CSharpMT4 uses to trade.

docs.title: Investor password
docs.text:
• View-only — see trades, balance and history, but cannot trade.
  • Useful for sharing performance or read-only monitoring tools.
  • Set it in MT4 via Tools → Options → Server → Change (Investor Password).

docs.title: 🏦 Choosing a broker (optional)
docs.text:
The MetaQuotes demo server is perfect for practice. For live trading later you might pick a specific broker for better conditions or regional support.

Not financial advice. Always do your own research.

Popular MT4 brokers: IC Markets, Pepperstone, OANDA, XM, RoboForex, FxPro.

What to look for:

  • ✅ Regulation — FCA, ASIC, CySEC, etc.
  • ✅ MT4 support — make sure they actually offer MT4 (not only MT5).
  • ✅ Demo account — free (note: demo accounts often expire after ~30 days of inactivity).
  • ✅ Good spreads — lower spreads = lower cost.
  • ✅ Responsive support — in your language.

docs.title: 1. Connect CSharpMT4
docs.text:
Follow the main setup guide to install, configure and run:

👉 Getting Started · Your First Project (10 min)

docs.title: 2. Learn the three layers
docs.text:
CSharpMT4 is built in three levels, low to high — pick where to start:

  • Level 1 — MT4Account: direct low-level gRPC calls. Maximum control; everything else is built on it.
  • Level 2 — MT4Service: typed wrappers over MT4Account. Clean signatures, ready data. Best for most scenarios.
  • Level 3 — MT4Sugar: convenience helpers (risk sizing, normalization, batch actions). Most beginner-friendly.

docs.title: 🛡️ Security
docs.text:
• Never share your master password. Use the investor password for monitoring tools.
  • Keep credentials safe (a password manager helps). Don't commit real credentials to source control.

docs.title: 📊 Risk management
docs.text: • Demo is risk-free, but build good habits: always use a stop-loss, don't risk more than 1–2% per trade, understand position sizing.

docs.title: 🧪 Testing
docs.text:
• Test all your code on demo first. Verify strategies over weeks, not days. Demo results don't guarantee live results.

Ready to code? Head to Getting Started and connect CSharpMT4 to your account. Good luck! 🚀

docs.title: 🗺️ CSharpMT4 Project Map
docs.text: The whole project as one annotated tree, with links. Links point to section overviews, never to individual method pages — open an overview to drill down into its methods.

docs.text:

Layer Source What it does Overview 3 · MT4Sugar MT4Sugar.cs Convenience on top of Service: risk-based sizing (CalcVolumeForRiskAsync, BuyMarketByRiskAsync), price/volume normalization, point-offset helpers, batch close/cancel. MT4Sugar overview · index 2 · MT4Service MT4Service.cs Typed facade: clean signatures that return ready data structures (no raw proto). What most code uses. MT4Service overview · index 1 · MT4Account package/Helpers/MT4Account.cs Low-level gRPC: proto request/reply, connect/session, auto-reconnect, streaming. Everything else builds on it. MT4Account overview · index 
Your code  →  MT4Sugar  →  MT4Service  →  MT4Account  →  gRPC  →  MetaRPC gateway → MT4 terminal
